data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Cycle & Carriage, Creative Technology, CNMC Goldmine
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Aug 21):

Jardine Cycle & Carriage (JC&C) : JC&C announced on Friday that it has entered into a conditional share and asset purchase agreement to sell its Cycle & Carriage automotive distribution and retail operations in Singapore and Malaysia to CCHPL Holdings, a wholly owned subsidiary of Indonesia’s Chandra Asri Pacific. The estimated base purchase price payable in cash is around S$265 million. Shares of JC&C ended at S$27.50 on Thursday, 1.2 per cent or S$0.32 higher.

Creative Technology : The technology group on Thursday posted net profit of US$649,000 for its second half ended Jun 30, compared with a net loss of US$4.38 million in the year-ago period. This was mainly due to a US$1.3 million US tariff refund. Excluding the refund, it would have resulted in a H2 net loss of US$600,000. For the full year, it still incurred a net loss, but it narrowed 94 per cent to a loss of US$576,000. Shares of Creative Technology ended at S$0.785 on Thursday, 0.6 per cent or S$0.005 lower, before the news.

data.title: Issue 208: Sembcorp’s turbulent week; nuclear financing’s green acceptance
data.description:
Sustainable investing

Sembcorp’s diversified portfolio saves the day

A diversified portfolio may have helped Sembcorp Industries to emerge from a roller-coaster week with a tailwind.

Shares of the renewable energy company took a beating before the Aug 15 weekend as a major index dropped the stock and lacklustre earnings reflected persistent weakness in China. However, the counter has bounced back even higher as an Australian acquisition and a potential spin-off in India give analysts and investors a positive story to buy.

data.title: Singapore stocks rise on Friday; STI up 0.3%
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore stocks ended higher on Friday (Aug 21).

The benchmark Straits Times Index (STI) gained 0.3 per cent or 17.05 points to finish at 5,688.96.

City Developments led the gainers on Singapore’s blue-chip index, rising 1.7 per cent or S$0.14 to S$8.25.

The worst performer among STI constituents was ST Engineering , which fell 1.6 per cent or S$0.17 to S$10.68.

The trio of local banks ended higher. DBS gained 0.2 per cent or S$0.16 to finish at S$76, OCBC rose 0.7 per cent or S$0.20 to S$30.98, and UOB was up 0.8 per cent or S$0.31 at S$40.53.

Within the iEdge Singapore Next 50 Index, First Resources was the top gainer, rising 3.3 per cent or S$0.14 to S$4.42, while UltraGreen.ai was the biggest decliner, falling 14.8 per cent or US$0.11 to US$0.635.

In the broader market, gainers outnumbered losers 322 to 242, after 1.1 billion securities worth S$2 billion changed hands.

International Cement Group was the most actively traded stock, with 47.3 million shares changing hands.

DBS was the most actively traded stock in terms of value, with a volume of 3.4 million shares worth S$255.8 million.

Key regional indices were mixed. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index gained 1.2 per cent and South Korea’s Kospi was up 0.9 per cent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.3 per cent and the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI was down 0.01 per cent.

Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management, said that the US Treasury’s move to increase the size of buybacks of longer-dated debt will matter for Asian markets.

A softer US dollar will loosen financial conditions in the region, give local central banks more “breathing room” and keep capital circulating through equities rather than being pulled relentlessly back towards US cash and Treasuries, he added.

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by a reporter

data.title: Where the real returns on Singapore’s deep-tech investments lie
data.description:
EVERY few years, Singapore asks a familiar question: Are we getting enough return from our investments in research and innovation?

It is a fair question. Taxpayers deserve to know whether decades of funding into science, startups and emerging technologies are creating lasting economic value.

Much of the debate focuses on visible outcomes – initial public offerings, unicorns, fundraising rounds and exits. These are important milestones, but they are also the final chapter of a much longer story.

data.title: Lily Ler to step down as CEO of Mapletree Industrial Trust manager
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The chief executive of Mapletree Industrial Trust Management, Lily Ler, is stepping down from her position to become group chief financial officer of Mapletree Investments, the trust’s sponsor.

She will vacate her roles as CEO and executive director on Oct 1, the manager said in a bourse filing on Friday (Aug 21).

Anand Tze Ming Chandran, currently head of Asia-Pacific data centres at Mapletree Investments, will succeed Ler as CEO and executive director of the trust’s manager.

His appointments will be effective from Oct 1 as well, subject to regulatory approval.

Chandran joined the sponsor in February after serving as CFO of K2 Strategic, the Kuok Group’s digital infrastructure platform. He has more than 16 years of experience across corporate finance, investment banking and digital infrastructure.

He holds degrees from the London School of Economics and Political Science, University of Oxford, as well as Singapore Management University.

Detailed disclosures regarding the management changes will be released separately, the manager of Mapletree Industrial Trust said.

The trust’s units closed at S$1.92 on Friday, up 0.5 per cent or S$0.01, before the news.

data.title: Digital Realty, STT GDC among data centre operators awarded 50 MW of new capacity in Singapore
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The Singapore government on Friday (Aug 21) awarded a total of 200 megawatts (MW) in new data centre capacity to four data centre operators in its latest tender.

The four – Digital Realty, Equinix, ST Telemedia Global Data Centres (STT GDC) and Keppel Data Centres – bagged the capacity under the Data Centre - Call For Application 2 (DC-CFA 2) tender.

They will each be provisionally allocated 50 MW of capacity, and locate their facilities on Jurong Island.

The Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) and Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) said in a statement: “To enable the data-centre sector to operate more sustainably, JTC is developing a low-carbon data centre park on Jurong Island to leverage potential low-carbon technology synergies within the island’s ecosystem.”

Keppel said that the data centre capacity will go towards the development of its newest AI-ready data centre, with an expected investment of more than S$1 billion.

The centre will be funded by its own private fund, the Keppel Data Centre Fund III, and funds from its co-investors, said the group in a statement.

Announced last December, the DC-CFA 2 exercise received more than 20 applications from local and global operators.

The supported data centres have committed to exceed the minimum sustainability requirements imposed in the latest rounds of the tender, said EDB and IMDA.

This means that the operators will power more than half their data centre capacity from green energy sources.

They will also be the “best-in-class” in energy efficiency by adopting advanced technologies such as liquid cooling and using 100 per cent energy-efficient IT equipment, the joint EDB-IMDA statement added.

Bruno Lopez, president and group CEO of STT GDC, said the group remains committed to using the Republic’s land, energy and water resources “prudently” to deliver “meaningful and lasting value” for Singapore.

He noted that the effects of STT GDC data centre would extend beyond computing powers, and that the group will translate the investment into “enduring economic value for Singapore, strengthen its digital ecosystem and international connectivity, and support the continued growth and vibrancy of its digital economy”.

Keppel said it would tap its “extensive capabilities” in data-centre, power, cooling, connectivity and low-carbon solutions, as well as its existing energy and utilities on Jurong Island, to support its facility.

It has 1,900 MW of power generation capacity in its Keppel Merlimau Cogen Plant and the Keppel Sakra Cogen plant, both on Jurong Island.

Digital Realty said that, beyond computing, it intends to continue investing in local talent and deepen partnerships to focus on its long-term digital growth.

“Our selection under DC-CFA2 will enable us to continue contributing to Singapore’s ambitions for responsible AI adoption and a resilient digital future,” it added.

Yee May Leong, managing director of Equinix Singapore, said: “Together, we can accelerate the growth of Singapore’s digital economy and strengthen its position as a trusted digital and AI hub for Asean and the world.”

All four selected data centre operators have an established presence in the country.

Information from their websites indicate that Digital Realty has three data centres in Singapore currently, and Equinix has five.

STT GDC has six data centres with an IT load of more than 110 MW, and Keppel Data Centres has eight.

The first DC-CFA exercise in July 2023 awarded 80 MW of new capacity to Equinix, GDS, Microsoft and an AirTrunk-ByteDance consortium.

EDB and IMDA will review the need for another DC-CFA in 18 to 24 months.

data.title: The ‘ultimate luxury’? Inside Singapore’s premium health boom
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] From the traditional environs of the golf course or country club, the Republic’s well-heeled are now heading to upscale gyms and paying five-figure fees for personal training plans.

The city’s luxury fitness industry is growing, with premium brands expanding their footprints in prime locations.

The move is part of a global trend, as what arguably began as a Silicon Valley niche – popularised by tech entrepreneurs like Bryan Johnson and his multi-million-dollar anti-ageing regimens – finds a lucrative foothold in Asia and elsewhere.

data.title: At Embed Financial, a big push to support sports that are inclusive
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Embed Financial Group Holdings (EFGH) is based in Singapore and designs and operates digital financial infrastructure across Asia and Africa.

But beyond its core business, the young company – founded a little over two years ago – is also going big on its support of sports in Singapore.

Last year, EFGH became the new title sponsor of the Tour de France Singapore Criterium, and it recently extended the partnership with this major cycling event for an additional three years until 2028.

In December, the EFGH National Championships will be a key feature of the BYD Singapore International Marathon with a beefed-up total prize pool of S$177,500. This marks the first time that the national championships will have a named sponsor since it was integrated into the annual marathon’s race weekend back in 2017.

And just two months ago, EFGH and the Singapore National Olympic Council announced a five-year sponsorship partnership to support Team Singapore athletes, along with a new awards initiative at the Singapore Sports Awards to recognise coaches.

BT Weekend visited EFGH’s office at Robinson Road where we met executive chairman Dennis Ng, a 54-year-old who previously held senior roles at Prudential, Allianz and Citi before he founded EFGH in 2024. This is an edited excerpt of the interview.

Tell me about the company and what you do.

We are what we call a “finternet” – or financial Internet – company. We are a digital financial infrastructure company valued at US$425 million and looking at a listing on a US exchange.

Since the start, we have always been about inclusive finance. We partner with governments, regulated financial institutions and enterprises to deploy embedded finance at scale.

Right now we are present in about nine markets in Africa, and we have two CEOs based there – one in Zimbabwe and one in Congo.

A lot of people in that continent are underinsured or not insured at all, and many are unbankable because 70 per cent of Africa’s economy is the informal economy.

We are going to expand to more areas in Asia, including South Korea and Japan. We are also talking to potential partners in Indonesia and Vietnam, and the whole idea is to serve the emerging markets as much as possible.

How did you decide to get so involved in sports events?

I would say that supporting globally recognised events in Singapore reflects our confidence in the nation’s role as a gateway city for business, sport and innovation. Our partnerships reflect a broader commitment to strengthening the sporting ecosystem – from supporting elite athlete development to contributing to the continued growth of major international sporting events here.

Quite often, it’s a foreign company that is a sporting event’s title sponsor so I felt that a Singapore company should lead the charge.

This is a chance for us to be part of a major event like the Tour de France which is broadcast to 150 countries or more. You look at these elite cyclists and the way they train with so much discipline. It’s similar to our business because to operate in the emerging markets, you need a lot of discipline and grit too.

What is it about the marathon that appeals to you?

The Singapore Marathon has always attracted large crowds and we see people come to Singapore and run long distances, which is not easy. You have to train hard and commit to the rigour. I’m not a marathon runner but I see my friends train for as long as eight months to make sure they are ready for the big day.

Betterment Sports – part of the joint venture that’s organising and promoting the Singapore Marathon – came to have a chat with me and I agreed we could do something together, because this event puts Singapore on the map.

Thousands of people take part, including many from overseas, and we have this opportunity to support it and interact with people from all over the world.

Running and cycling are the two most popular sports in Singapore and many other countries too.

It’s about us wanting to be inclusive. We want to make sure every person can have access to simple financial tools. Running and cycling, as you have correctly pointed out, are both very inclusive. You have a pair of shoes, you’re good to go. You have a bicycle, you’re good to go. We could have picked something like golf, but at the end of the day it’s a sport that only a small segment of the population plays.

Are you an active person yourself?

I’m a weekend warrior, the furthest I can run these days is 5 km, and sometimes I end up walking (laughs). I enjoy running at the East Coast Park area which is close to where I live.

There’s a fixed route that I do. I try not to deviate from it because I might lose track of the distance. Running helps me to clear my mind, and it’s not just about the cardio.
